drills.q: What are MCTS's four phases, in order?
Roughly how many legal moves does Go have per position on average, versus chess?
True or false: MCTS, once search completes, executes its entire most-visited simulated line of moves before replanning.
drills.a: False -- MCTS commits to only the single immediate real action with the highest visit count at the root, then discards the tree and replans fresh from the new real state.

drills.q: Write the UCT formula and identify which part of it comes from the UCB1 bandit algorithm.
drills.a: UCT(s,a) = Q(s,a) + c*sqrt(ln N(s)/N(s,a)). The entire exploration term (the sqrt confidence-bound expression) is a direct instantiation of UCB1's bandit exploration bonus, applied at every node by treating each node's children as an independent multi-armed bandit.

drills.q: What replaces the random rollout in AlphaZero, and why is that a variance improvement, not just a speed improvement?
drills.a: A learned value/policy network f_theta(s) -> (p(.|s), v(s)) replaces the rollout. A random playout to a game's end is an extremely high-variance, weakly-informative signal, while a trained value network gives a much lower-variance point estimate in one forward pass, having learned correlations with actual outcomes across many training games.

drills.q: A Dyna-Q implementation trains slower than plain model-free Q-learning on the same task. What's the likely cause?
drills.a: The learned model is a poor approximation of the true dynamics (common early in training or in rarely-visited states), so simulated updates are training the Q-function toward a systematically wrong target -- the same failure signature as DQN's 'stable loss, wrong bootstrap target' problem, just introduced via the model instead of a stale target network.

drills.q: Explain why PUCT's prior term p(s,a) is especially important for a game like Go rather than a lower-branching-factor game.
drills.a: With ~250 legal moves per position, uniformly exploring every child a few times before any accumulates meaningful statistics (pure UCT's early behavior) wastes an enormous fraction of a realistic simulation budget. PUCT's prior immediately concentrates search on the subset of moves the policy network already considers promising, which matters far more when the branching factor is large.

drills.q: Derive, informally, why compounding model error is a fundamentally different problem from one-step model prediction error, and state the practical mitigation.
drills.a: A model with per-step error epsilon produces rollout divergence that grows roughly with horizon times epsilon in a favorable case, and worse when small errors push the trajectory out-of-distribution for the model (a further, self-reinforcing error source). One-step accuracy says nothing about whether multi-step errors compound benignly or catastrophically. Mitigation: short planning horizons with frequent replanning against real observations, rather than long open-loop plans.

drills.q: Compare the role of a learned value function in AlphaZero's MCTS versus PPO's critic. Are they serving the same purpose?
drills.a: Related but structurally different. PPO's critic shapes a bootstrapped advantage estimate used to compute a gradient for training the actor's parameters -- it doesn't directly select actions at decision time. AlphaZero's value network is used INSIDE the search itself, at decision time, to estimate leaf-node values that directly influence which branches get explored and which real action is ultimately chosen.

drills.q: Design a model-based path-planning system for a warehouse robot sharing space with unpredictable human workers. What planning horizon and replanning frequency should you use, and why?
drills.a: Short planning horizon with frequent (ideally every real step) replanning, MPC-style. The map's deterministic portions can be modeled and planned through accurately, but the unpredictable elements (human/robot movement) are exactly where model predictions are least reliable, and errors there compound fastest in the parts of the plan furthest from the current observed real state -- frequent replanning lets real observations correct the plan before that error compounds.

drills.q: A colleague claims model-based RL is strictly more sample-efficient than model-free RL with no real downside. Push back with the specific mechanism.
drills.a: Model-based sample efficiency is conditional on model accuracy, not unconditional. A learned model's compounding error over multi-step rollouts or planning can train a value function or select actions against a systematically wrong picture of the world -- a risk pure model-free methods never carry, since they never extrapolate through a learned dynamics model. The efficiency gain is real but must be weighed against this qualitatively different failure mode plus the added engineering cost of maintaining and validating a second learned system (the model).
